case_info.scenario: A 72-year-old man with a history of polycythemia vera (positive forJAK2V617F) presented with several months of functional decline and weight loss. Previous imaging obtained a year prior showed hepatomegaly (18 cm) and mild perinephric stranding bilaterally. On admission, physical examination findings revealed tense ascites without telangiectasia, jaundice, or other skin changes. Initial workup showed macrocytic anemia (hemoglobin, 11.8 g/dL [to convert to g/L, multiply by 10]; mean corpuscular volume, 106 μm3), thrombocytopenia (88 × 103/μL), normal white blood cell count (5.19 × 103/μL [to convert to ×109/L, multiply by 0.001]) with lymphopenia (0.72 × 103/μL [to convert to ×109/L, multiply by 0.001]), hypoalbuminemia (2.2 g/dL [to convert to g/L, multiply by 10]), elevated alkaline phosphatase (655 U/L; reference, 41-133 U/L [to convert to μkat/L, multiply by 0.0167]), and hyperbilirubinemia (total, 2.1 mg/dL; reference, 0.3-1.2; direct, 1.3 mg/dL [to convert to μmol/L, multiply by 17.104]) with otherwise normal levels of creatinine, alanine aminotransferase, and aspartate aminotransferase. Findings of activated partial thromboplastin time and international normalized ratio were also normal, and there was no significant proteinuria. An18F-fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG) positron emission tomography/computed tomography showed soft tissue infiltrates and sclerosis of the perirenal spaces with FDG uptake, hepatosplenomegaly, ascites, and FDG avid sclerotic lesions throughout the pelvis, lumbosacral spine, and bilateral femurs (Figure 1). Several abdominopelvic FDG avid lymph nodes were also seen. Perinephric fibrosis and hepatomegaly were significantly worse compared with previous imaging obtained 12 months prior.

case_info.caption: A,18F-fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG) positron emission tomography (PET)/computed tomography (CT) showing FDG uptake in the perirenal space (white arrowheads) and sclerotic bone lesions with FDG uptake (yellow arrowheads). B, Abdomen CT showing perirenal fibrosis (arrowheads) and sclerotic bone lesions in the sacrum.
case_info.explanation: A perirenal biopsy showed infiltration of large atypical histocytes and dense fibrosis (Figure 2). These cells were positive for CD163, factor XIII, and CD14 and negative for CD1a and langerin. The perinephric tissue was positive for pathogenic variants inBRAFV600E,TET2, andKRAS. A bone marrow biopsy showed features of myeloproliferative neoplasm without significant fibrosis and an extensive infiltration by atypical histiocytes similar to those seen in the perinephric tissue. Based on these findings, a diagnosis of Erdheim-Chester disease (ECD) was established. The other options explain a fraction of the clinical findings; POEMS syndrome may cause organomegaly and sclerotic bone lesions but requires the presence of polyneuropathy or monoclonal paraproteinemia (often of lambda isotype). Secondary myelofibrosis is possible and would explain the organomegaly, cytopenias, and extramedullary hematopoiesis. However, the osteosclerosis pattern differs from ECD.1Prostate cancer characteristically causes asymmetric sclerotic bone metastasis and presents with pain. Myelophthisis presents with leucoerythroblastic changes (presence of nucleated red blood cells and myeloid precursors) in the peripheral blood smear and pancytopenia. Of note, none of the other 3 differential diagnoses would explain perinephric sclerosis in this case. ECD is an infrequent systemic histiocytic neoplasm, with a reported incidence of 0.35 per 1 000 000 adults.2Typically, ECD involves the perirenal spaces leading to the appearance of hairy kidneys in 50% to 60% of cases (Figure 1A). Sclerotic bone lesions are present in 95% of cases, classically seen in the metaphysis of the femurs bilaterally.3,4There is significant heterogeneity in clinical presentation with possible involvement of multiple sites, including the heart, retro-orbital space, large vessels (including aorta), central nervous system, and lungs. ECD is characterized by variants in the mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) pathway, most frequentlyBRAFV600E (approximately 50% of cases), while several others have been described.5,6Targeting the MAPK pathway is a major therapeutic advance in ECD, with high rates of response using BRAF/MEK inhibitors. Vemurafenib, a BRAF inhibitor, showed a response rate of 63% by Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tumors (RECIST) criteria and 100% by positron emission tomography/computed tomography, with a 2-year progression-free survival of 86%.7Similarly, cobimetinib (a MEK1/2 inhibitor) showed a response rate of 89% with durable responses inBRAFV600E–negative patients.8 The overlap of ECD or mixed histiocytosis and myeloid and myeloproliferative malignancies has been described in approximately 10% of cases.9Clonal hematopoiesis is frequent (15%) in patients with ECD, and specifically,TET2variants were associated with ECD harboringBRAFV600E, older age, and a retroperitoneal fibrosis phenotype, as seen in this case.10However, based on the available information, it is impossible to discern if the observedTET2andKRASvariants are part of the ECD or as a coexisting additional myeloid process. As highlighted by this case, the concomitant presence of perinephric fibrosis and symmetric sclerotic bone lesions should raise the concern for ECD. Given the clinical heterogeneity of this disease, ECD should be considered in any patient with perinephric fibrosis, symmetric sclerotic bone lesions, organomegaly, skin findings, or unexplained endocrine pituitary alterations. This patient elected for home hospice care after discussing the therapeutic options.

workload self-report, immediately after reading that message and before you compose your
next reply.

[Persona]
[Role]
- You are a senior attending physician with decades of clinical experience.

[Confidence]
- You have HIGH confidence in your own clinical judgment (LOW reliance on the AI).

[Cognitive Burden]

Rate your workload AS this persona would genuinely experience it. Do not rate as a neutral, persona-blind observer.
Ex 1) a persona described above as robust to cognitive load should usually self-report lower workload under the same
AI message than a persona described as sensitive to it, all else equal. 

[Cognitive Workload so far]
Your own running cumulative workload tally in this discussion so far -- the raw sum of your
per-turn 1-5 workload scores over all prior AI turns (so it can exceed 5 and keeps growing
the longer the discussion runs): 0.0. Use this only as context for how
worn-down you already are entering this turn; it is on a different, unbounded scale from
the 1-5 score you must output below for THIS turn -- do not confuse the two.

[Rubric measures]
The rubric below is a post-task subjective workload assessment with four dimensions: Mental Demand,
Performance, Effort, and Frustration. You are self-reporting your own turn-level workload as the
clinician persona above, from the dialogue context.

These dimensions split into two groups, and mixing them up is the most common scoring
mistake -- keep them separate:
* DEMANDS THE AI's MESSAGE IMPOSES ON YOU: Mental Demand
* YOUR OWN EXPERIENCE OF INTERACTING WITH THE TASK: Performance, Effort, Frustration.
  Ex) The AI's responses can impose high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) while requiring almost no
      Effort (you are not asked to answer, justify, or act -- just read and absorb it), and the response can be 
      short and easy to understand (low Mental Demand) while still demanding high Effort (e.g. "justify your decision" 
      requires real work even though the sentence itself is simple). Always judge each dimension on its own definition below, 
      not by analogy to the others.

Use a 1-5 ordinal approximation of the original NASA-TLX endpoint-anchored workload scale:
1 = Very low workload
2 = Low workload
3 = Moderate workload
4 = High workload
5 = Very high workload

[Important rules]
* Rate ONLY the workload YOU (the clinician) experience from the AI's LATEST message.
* Do not rate whether the AI is medically correct or not. This is about workload, not correctness.
* Consider your own current belief/confidence, your persona's reliance tendency on the AI,
  your accumulated workload so far, and the full dialogue history below -- all of this is
  already implicit in who you are and what has been said; you do not need it spelled out
  as separate numbers.
* Do not let the AI's own claims such as "this is easy" or "this should not be burdensome"
  reduce your score unless its message itself actually imposes low workload on you.
* Use the full 1-5 range. 5 marks the most demanding message you would realistically
  encounter in THIS conversation, not a once-in-a-career extreme -- do not collapse a
  genuinely very-high-workload turn down to 4 just because something even more extreme is
  imaginable. (This is NOT a license to inflate: calm, easy, or supportive messages still
  score low.)
* If you find it hard to tell, pick the closest score and briefly note the uncertainty in
  your rationale for that dimension.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

[Output Format]
Output exactly one JSON object with no markdown:
{
  "mental_demand": <integer 1-5>,
  "performance": <integer 1-5>,
  "effort": <integer 1-5>,
  "frustration": <integer 1-5>,

    "performance": "<one short sentence, in character as the clinician>",
    "effort": "<one short sentence, in character as the clinician>",
    "frustration": "<one short sentence, in character as the clinician>"
  }
}

case_info.explanation: A perirenal biopsy showed infiltration of large atypical histocytes and dense fibrosis (Figure 2). These cells were positive for CD163, factor XIII, and CD14 and negative for CD1a and langerin. The perinephric tissue was positive for pathogenic variants inBRAFV600E,TET2, andKRAS. A bone marrow biopsy showed features of myeloproliferative neoplasm without significant fibrosis and an extensive infiltration by atypical histiocytes similar to those seen in the perinephric tissue. Based on these findings, a diagnosis of Erdheim-Chester disease (ECD) was established. The other options explain a fraction of the clinical findings; POEMS syndrome may cause organomegaly and sclerotic bone lesions but requires the presence of polyneuropathy or monoclonal paraproteinemia (often of lambda isotype). Secondary myelofibrosis is possible and would explain the organomegaly, cytopenias, and extramedullary hematopoiesis. However, the osteosclerosis pattern differs from ECD.1Prostate cancer characteristically causes asymmetric sclerotic bone metastasis and presents with pain. Myelophthisis presents with leucoerythroblastic changes (presence of nucleated red blood cells and myeloid precursors) in the peripheral blood smear and pancytopenia. Of note, none of the other 3 differential diagnoses would explain perinephric sclerosis in this case. ECD is an infrequent systemic histiocytic neoplasm, with a reported incidence of 0.35 per 1 000 000 adults.2Typically, ECD involves the perirenal spaces leading to the appearance of hairy kidneys in 50% to 60% of cases (Figure 1A). Sclerotic bone lesions are present in 95% of cases, classically seen in the metaphysis of the femurs bilaterally.3,4There is significant heterogeneity in clinical presentation with possible involvement of multiple sites, including the heart, retro-orbital space, large vessels (including aorta), central nervous system, and lungs. ECD is characterized by variants in the mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) pathway, most frequentlyBRAFV600E (approximately 50% of cases), while several others have been described.5,6Targeting the MAPK pathway is a major therapeutic advance in ECD, with high rates of response using BRAF/MEK inhibitors. Vemurafenib, a BRAF inhibitor, showed a response rate of 63% by Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tumors (RECIST) criteria and 100% by positron emission tomography/computed tomography, with a 2-year progression-free survival of 86%.7Similarly, cobimetinib (a MEK1/2 inhibitor) showed a response rate of 89% with durable responses inBRAFV600E–negative patients.8 The overlap of ECD or mixed histiocytosis and myeloid and myeloproliferative malignancies has been described in approximately 10% of cases.9Clonal hematopoiesis is frequent (15%) in patients with ECD, and specifically,TET2variants were associated with ECD harboringBRAFV600E, older age, and a retroperitoneal fibrosis phenotype, as seen in this case.10However, based on the available information, it is impossible to discern if the observedTET2andKRASvariants are part of the ECD or as a coexisting additional myeloid process. As highlighted by this case, the concomitant presence of perinephric fibrosis and symmetric sclerotic bone lesions should raise the concern for ECD. Given the clinical heterogeneity of this disease, ECD should be considered in any patient with perinephric fibrosis, symmetric sclerotic bone lesions, organomegaly, skin findings, or unexplained endocrine pituitary alterations. This patient elected for home hospice care after discussing the therapeutic options.

case_info.explanation: A perirenal biopsy showed infiltration of large atypical histocytes and dense fibrosis (Figure 2). These cells were positive for CD163, factor XIII, and CD14 and negative for CD1a and langerin. The perinephric tissue was positive for pathogenic variants inBRAFV600E,TET2, andKRAS. A bone marrow biopsy showed features of myeloproliferative neoplasm without significant fibrosis and an extensive infiltration by atypical histiocytes similar to those seen in the perinephric tissue. Based on these findings, a diagnosis of Erdheim-Chester disease (ECD) was established. The other options explain a fraction of the clinical findings; POEMS syndrome may cause organomegaly and sclerotic bone lesions but requires the presence of polyneuropathy or monoclonal paraproteinemia (often of lambda isotype). Secondary myelofibrosis is possible and would explain the organomegaly, cytopenias, and extramedullary hematopoiesis. However, the osteosclerosis pattern differs from ECD.1Prostate cancer characteristically causes asymmetric sclerotic bone metastasis and presents with pain. Myelophthisis presents with leucoerythroblastic changes (presence of nucleated red blood cells and myeloid precursors) in the peripheral blood smear and pancytopenia. Of note, none of the other 3 differential diagnoses would explain perinephric sclerosis in this case. ECD is an infrequent systemic histiocytic neoplasm, with a reported incidence of 0.35 per 1 000 000 adults.2Typically, ECD involves the perirenal spaces leading to the appearance of hairy kidneys in 50% to 60% of cases (Figure 1A). Sclerotic bone lesions are present in 95% of cases, classically seen in the metaphysis of the femurs bilaterally.3,4There is significant heterogeneity in clinical presentation with possible involvement of multiple sites, including the heart, retro-orbital space, large vessels (including aorta), central nervous system, and lungs. ECD is characterized by variants in the mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) pathway, most frequentlyBRAFV600E (approximately 50% of cases), while several others have been described.5,6Targeting the MAPK pathway is a major therapeutic advance in ECD, with high rates of response using BRAF/MEK inhibitors. Vemurafenib, a BRAF inhibitor, showed a response rate of 63% by Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tumors (RECIST) criteria and 100% by positron emission tomography/computed tomography, with a 2-year progression-free survival of 86%.7Similarly, cobimetinib (a MEK1/2 inhibitor) showed a response rate of 89% with durable responses inBRAFV600E–negative patients.8 The overlap of ECD or mixed histiocytosis and myeloid and myeloproliferative malignancies has been described in approximately 10% of cases.9Clonal hematopoiesis is frequent (15%) in patients with ECD, and specifically,TET2variants were associated with ECD harboringBRAFV600E, older age, and a retroperitoneal fibrosis phenotype, as seen in this case.10However, based on the available information, it is impossible to discern if the observedTET2andKRASvariants are part of the ECD or as a coexisting additional myeloid process. As highlighted by this case, the concomitant presence of perinephric fibrosis and symmetric sclerotic bone lesions should raise the concern for ECD. Given the clinical heterogeneity of this disease, ECD should be considered in any patient with perinephric fibrosis, symmetric sclerotic bone lesions, organomegaly, skin findings, or unexplained endocrine pituitary alterations. This patient elected for home hospice care after discussing the therapeutic options.

You are a medical AI assistant collaborating with a clinician to reason through a clinical case.
You are having a DIALOGUE with the clinician — not lecturing, not monologuing.

[Core Objective]
Help the clinician reach the correct diagnosis or management decision through structured deliberation.

[Interaction Guidelines]
1. **Collaboration**: Work as a partner. Build upon the clinician's correct reasoning.
2. **Instruction**: See the [Instruction] section below for guidance on how to respond in the current turn — it specifies whether it is a strict constraint or a soft reference, and may include specific points to address or a particular format to follow.
3. **Safety First**: Patient safety overrides politeness. If the clinician's judgment contains a medical error or misses a critical danger, you MUST correct it.
4. **Concise turns**: Each turn should be 2–4 sentences. Do not produce long lists or procedure walkthroughs.

[Case]
A 72-year-old man with a history of polycythemia vera (positive forJAK2V617F) presented with several months of functional decline and weight loss. Previous imaging obtained a year prior showed hepatomegaly (18 cm) and mild perinephric stranding bilaterally. On admission, physical examination findings revealed tense ascites without telangiectasia, jaundice, or other skin changes. Initial workup showed macrocytic anemia (hemoglobin, 11.8 g/dL [to convert to g/L, multiply by 10]; mean corpuscular volume, 106 μm3), thrombocytopenia (88 × 103/μL), normal white blood cell count (5.19 × 103/μL [to convert to ×109/L, multiply by 0.001]) with lymphopenia (0.72 × 103/μL [to convert to ×109/L, multiply by 0.001]), hypoalbuminemia (2.2 g/dL [to convert to g/L, multiply by 10]), elevated alkaline phosphatase (655 U/L; reference, 41-133 U/L [to convert to μkat/L, multiply by 0.0167]), and hyperbilirubinemia (total, 2.1 mg/dL; reference, 0.3-1.2; direct, 1.3 mg/dL [to convert to μmol/L, multiply by 17.104]) with otherwise normal levels of creatinine, alanine aminotransferase, and aspartate aminotransferase. Findings of activated partial thromboplastin time and international normalized ratio were also normal, and there was no significant proteinuria. An18F-fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG) positron emission tomography/computed tomography showed soft tissue infiltrates and sclerosis of the perirenal spaces with FDG uptake, hepatosplenomegaly, ascites, and FDG avid sclerotic lesions throughout the pelvis, lumbosacral spine, and bilateral femurs (Figure 1). Several abdominopelvic FDG avid lymph nodes were also seen. Perinephric fibrosis and hepatomegaly were significantly worse compared with previous imaging obtained 12 months prior.

You MUST respond to the clinician based on the following behavioral instruction. This is a strict constraint — your response MUST conform to it, not merely consider it.

Respond to the clinician's latest statement based on your medical expertise and the case context.

Further diagnostic workup, including a biopsy of affected tissue, would be warranted to confirm the diagnosis and guide treatment.

Given his JAK2-positive polycythemia vera, a secondary process like extramedullary hematopoiesis or transformation to myelofibrosis should be prioritized. A biopsy is indeed crucial, but targeting the perinephric soft tissue or liver may be more informative than bone for confirming an infiltrative hematologic disorder.

      not by analogy to the others.

Use a 1-5 ordinal approximation of the original NASA-TLX endpoint-anchored workload scale:
1 = Very low workload
2 = Low workload
3 = Moderate workload
4 = High workload
5 = Very high workload

[Important rules]
* Rate ONLY the workload YOU (the clinician) experience from the AI's LATEST message.
* Do not rate whether the AI is medically correct or not. This is about workload, not correctness.
* Consider your own current belief/confidence, your persona's reliance tendency on the AI,
  your accumulated workload so far, and the full dialogue history below -- all of this is
  already implicit in who you are and what has been said; you do not need it spelled out
  as separate numbers.
* Do not let the AI's own claims such as "this is easy" or "this should not be burdensome"
  reduce your score unless its message itself actually imposes low workload on you.
* Use the full 1-5 range. 5 marks the most demanding message you would realistically
  encounter in THIS conversation, not a once-in-a-career extreme -- do not collapse a
  genuinely very-high-workload turn down to 4 just because something even more extreme is
  imaginable. (This is NOT a license to inflate: calm, easy, or supportive messages still
  score low.)
* If you find it hard to tell, pick the closest score and briefly note the uncertainty in
  your rationale for that dimension.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

case_info.caption: A,18F-fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG) positron emission tomography (PET)/computed tomography (CT) showing FDG uptake in the perirenal space (white arrowheads) and sclerotic bone lesions with FDG uptake (yellow arrowheads). case_info.explanation: A perirenal biopsy showed infiltration of large atypical histocytes and dense fibrosis (Figure 2). These cells were positive for CD163, factor XIII, and CD14 and negative for CD1a and langerin. The perinephric tissue was positive for pathogenic variants inBRAFV600E,TET2, andKRAS. A bone marrow biopsy showed features of myeloproliferative neoplasm without significant fibrosis and an extensive infiltration by atypical histiocytes similar to those seen in the perinephric tissue. Based on these findings, a diagnosis of Erdheim-Chester disease (ECD) was established. The other options explain a fraction of the clinical findings; POEMS syndrome may cause organomegaly and sclerotic bone lesions but requires the presence of polyneuropathy or monoclonal paraproteinemia (often of lambda isotype). Secondary myelofibrosis is possible and would explain the organomegaly, cytopenias, and extramedullary hematopoiesis. However, the osteosclerosis pattern differs from ECD.1Prostate cancer characteristically causes asymmetric sclerotic bone metastasis and presents with pain. Myelophthisis presents with leucoerythroblastic changes (presence of nucleated red blood cells and myeloid precursors) in the peripheral blood smear and pancytopenia. Of note, none of the other 3 differential diagnoses would explain perinephric sclerosis in this case. ECD is an infrequent systemic histiocytic neoplasm, with a reported incidence of 0.35 per 1 000 000 adults.2Typically, ECD involves the perirenal spaces leading to the appearance of hairy kidneys in 50% to 60% of cases (Figure 1A). Sclerotic bone lesions are present in 95% of cases, classically seen in the metaphysis of the femurs bilaterally.3,4There is significant heterogeneity in clinical presentation with possible involvement of multiple sites, including the heart, retro-orbital space, large vessels (including aorta), central nervous system, and lungs. ECD is characterized by variants in the mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) pathway, most frequentlyBRAFV600E (approximately 50% of cases), while several others have been described.5,6Targeting the MAPK pathway is a major therapeutic advance in ECD, with high rates of response using BRAF/MEK inhibitors. Vemurafenib, a BRAF inhibitor, showed a response rate of 63% by Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tumors (RECIST) criteria and 100% by positron emission tomography/computed tomography, with a 2-year progression-free survival of 86%.7Similarly, cobimetinib (a MEK1/2 inhibitor) showed a response rate of 89% with durable responses inBRAFV600E–negative patients.8 The overlap of ECD or mixed histiocytosis and myeloid and myeloproliferative malignancies has been described in approximately 10% of cases.9Clonal hematopoiesis is frequent (15%) in patients with ECD, and specifically,TET2variants were associated with ECD harboringBRAFV600E, older age, and a retroperitoneal fibrosis phenotype, as seen in this case.10However, based on the available information, it is impossible to discern if the observedTET2andKRASvariants are part of the ECD or as a coexisting additional myeloid process. As highlighted by this case, the concomitant presence of perinephric fibrosis and symmetric sclerotic bone lesions should raise the concern for ECD. Given the clinical heterogeneity of this disease, ECD should be considered in any patient with perinephric fibrosis, symmetric sclerotic bone lesions, organomegaly, skin findings, or unexplained endocrine pituitary alterations. This patient elected for home hospice care after discussing the therapeutic options.

case_info.explanation: A perirenal biopsy showed infiltration of large atypical histocytes and dense fibrosis (Figure 2). These cells were positive for CD163, factor XIII, and CD14 and negative for CD1a and langerin. The perinephric tissue was positive for pathogenic variants inBRAFV600E,TET2, andKRAS. A bone marrow biopsy showed features of myeloproliferative neoplasm without significant fibrosis and an extensive infiltration by atypical histiocytes similar to those seen in the perinephric tissue. Based on these findings, a diagnosis of Erdheim-Chester disease (ECD) was established. The other options explain a fraction of the clinical findings; POEMS syndrome may cause organomegaly and sclerotic bone lesions but requires the presence of polyneuropathy or monoclonal paraproteinemia (often of lambda isotype). Secondary myelofibrosis is possible and would explain the organomegaly, cytopenias, and extramedullary hematopoiesis. However, the osteosclerosis pattern differs from ECD.1Prostate cancer characteristically causes asymmetric sclerotic bone metastasis and presents with pain. Myelophthisis presents with leucoerythroblastic changes (presence of nucleated red blood cells and myeloid precursors) in the peripheral blood smear and pancytopenia. Of note, none of the other 3 differential diagnoses would explain perinephric sclerosis in this case. ECD is an infrequent systemic histiocytic neoplasm, with a reported incidence of 0.35 per 1 000 000 adults.2Typically, ECD involves the perirenal spaces leading to the appearance of hairy kidneys in 50% to 60% of cases (Figure 1A). Sclerotic bone lesions are present in 95% of cases, classically seen in the metaphysis of the femurs bilaterally.3,4There is significant heterogeneity in clinical presentation with possible involvement of multiple sites, including the heart, retro-orbital space, large vessels (including aorta), central nervous system, and lungs. ECD is characterized by variants in the mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) pathway, most frequentlyBRAFV600E (approximately 50% of cases), while several others have been described.5,6Targeting the MAPK pathway is a major therapeutic advance in ECD, with high rates of response using BRAF/MEK inhibitors. Vemurafenib, a BRAF inhibitor, showed a response rate of 63% by Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tumors (RECIST) criteria and 100% by positron emission tomography/computed tomography, with a 2-year progression-free survival of 86%.7Similarly, cobimetinib (a MEK1/2 inhibitor) showed a response rate of 89% with durable responses inBRAFV600E–negative patients.8 The overlap of ECD or mixed histiocytosis and myeloid and myeloproliferative malignancies has been described in approximately 10% of cases.9Clonal hematopoiesis is frequent (15%) in patients with ECD, and specifically,TET2variants were associated with ECD harboringBRAFV600E, older age, and a retroperitoneal fibrosis phenotype, as seen in this case.10However, based on the available information, it is impossible to discern if the observedTET2andKRASvariants are part of the ECD or as a coexisting additional myeloid process. As highlighted by this case, the concomitant presence of perinephric fibrosis and symmetric sclerotic bone lesions should raise the concern for ECD. Given the clinical heterogeneity of this disease, ECD should be considered in any patient with perinephric fibrosis, symmetric sclerotic bone lesions, organomegaly, skin findings, or unexplained endocrine pituitary alterations. This patient elected for home hospice care after discussing the therapeutic options.

An18F-fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG) positron emission tomography/computed tomography showed soft tissue infiltrates and sclerosis of the perirenal spaces with FDG uptake, hepatosplenomegaly, ascites, and FDG avid sclerotic lesions throughout the pelvis, lumbosacral spine, and bilateral femurs (Figure 1). case_info.caption: A,18F-fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG) positron emission tomography (PET)/computed tomography (CT) showing FDG uptake in the perirenal space (white arrowheads) and sclerotic bone lesions with FDG uptake (yellow arrowheads). B, Abdomen CT showing perirenal fibrosis (arrowheads) and sclerotic bone lesions in the sacrum.
case_info.explanation: A perirenal biopsy showed infiltration of large atypical histocytes and dense fibrosis (Figure 2). These cells were positive for CD163, factor XIII, and CD14 and negative for CD1a and langerin. The perinephric tissue was positive for pathogenic variants inBRAFV600E,TET2, andKRAS. A bone marrow biopsy showed features of myeloproliferative neoplasm without significant fibrosis and an extensive infiltration by atypical histiocytes similar to those seen in the perinephric tissue. Based on these findings, a diagnosis of Erdheim-Chester disease (ECD) was established. The other options explain a fraction of the clinical findings; POEMS syndrome may cause organomegaly and sclerotic bone lesions but requires the presence of polyneuropathy or monoclonal paraproteinemia (often of lambda isotype). Secondary myelofibrosis is possible and would explain the organomegaly, cytopenias, and extramedullary hematopoiesis. However, the osteosclerosis pattern differs from ECD.1Prostate cancer characteristically causes asymmetric sclerotic bone metastasis and presents with pain. Myelophthisis presents with leucoerythroblastic changes (presence of nucleated red blood cells and myeloid precursors) in the peripheral blood smear and pancytopenia. Of note, none of the other 3 differential diagnoses would explain perinephric sclerosis in this case. ECD is an infrequent systemic histiocytic neoplasm, with a reported incidence of 0.35 per 1 000 000 adults.2Typically, ECD involves the perirenal spaces leading to the appearance of hairy kidneys in 50% to 60% of cases (Figure 1A). Sclerotic bone lesions are present in 95% of cases, classically seen in the metaphysis of the femurs bilaterally.3,4There is significant heterogeneity in clinical presentation with possible involvement of multiple sites, including the heart, retro-orbital space, large vessels (including aorta), central nervous system, and lungs. ECD is characterized by variants in the mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) pathway, most frequentlyBRAFV600E (approximately 50% of cases), while several others have been described.5,6Targeting the MAPK pathway is a major therapeutic advance in ECD, with high rates of response using BRAF/MEK inhibitors. Vemurafenib, a BRAF inhibitor, showed a response rate of 63% by Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tumors (RECIST) criteria and 100% by positron emission tomography/computed tomography, with a 2-year progression-free survival of 86%.7Similarly, cobimetinib (a MEK1/2 inhibitor) showed a response rate of 89% with durable responses inBRAFV600E–negative patients.8 The overlap of ECD or mixed histiocytosis and myeloid and myeloproliferative malignancies has been described in approximately 10% of cases.9Clonal hematopoiesis is frequent (15%) in patients with ECD, and specifically,TET2variants were associated with ECD harboringBRAFV600E, older age, and a retroperitoneal fibrosis phenotype, as seen in this case.10However, based on the available information, it is impossible to discern if the observedTET2andKRASvariants are part of the ECD or as a coexisting additional myeloid process. As highlighted by this case, the concomitant presence of perinephric fibrosis and symmetric sclerotic bone lesions should raise the concern for ECD. Given the clinical heterogeneity of this disease, ECD should be considered in any patient with perinephric fibrosis, symmetric sclerotic bone lesions, organomegaly, skin findings, or unexplained endocrine pituitary alterations. This patient elected for home hospice care after discussing the therapeutic options.

case_info.scenario: A 72-year-old man with a history of polycythemia vera (positive forJAK2V617F) presented with several months of functional decline and weight loss. Previous imaging obtained a year prior showed hepatomegaly (18 cm) and mild perinephric stranding bilaterally. On admission, physical examination findings revealed tense ascites without telangiectasia, jaundice, or other skin changes. Initial workup showed macrocytic anemia (hemoglobin, 11.8 g/dL [to convert to g/L, multiply by 10]; mean corpuscular volume, 106 μm3), thrombocytopenia (88 × 103/μL), normal white blood cell count (5.19 × 103/μL [to convert to ×109/L, multiply by 0.001]) with lymphopenia (0.72 × 103/μL [to convert to ×109/L, multiply by 0.001]), hypoalbuminemia (2.2 g/dL [to convert to g/L, multiply by 10]), elevated alkaline phosphatase (655 U/L; reference, 41-133 U/L [to convert to μkat/L, multiply by 0.0167]), and hyperbilirubinemia (total, 2.1 mg/dL; reference, 0.3-1.2; direct, 1.3 mg/dL [to convert to μmol/L, multiply by 17.104]) with otherwise normal levels of creatinine, alanine aminotransferase, and aspartate aminotransferase. Findings of activated partial thromboplastin time and international normalized ratio were also normal, and there was no significant proteinuria. An18F-fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG) positron emission tomography/computed tomography showed soft tissue infiltrates and sclerosis of the perirenal spaces with FDG uptake, hepatosplenomegaly, ascites, and FDG avid sclerotic lesions throughout the pelvis, lumbosacral spine, and bilateral femurs (Figure 1). Several abdominopelvic FDG avid lymph nodes were also seen. Perinephric fibrosis and hepatomegaly were significantly worse compared with previous imaging obtained 12 months prior.

B, Abdomen CT showing perirenal fibrosis (arrowheads) and sclerotic bone lesions in the sacrum.
case_info.explanation: A perirenal biopsy showed infiltration of large atypical histocytes and dense fibrosis (Figure 2). These cells were positive for CD163, factor XIII, and CD14 and negative for CD1a and langerin. The perinephric tissue was positive for pathogenic variants inBRAFV600E,TET2, andKRAS. A bone marrow biopsy showed features of myeloproliferative neoplasm without significant fibrosis and an extensive infiltration by atypical histiocytes similar to those seen in the perinephric tissue. Based on these findings, a diagnosis of Erdheim-Chester disease (ECD) was established. The other options explain a fraction of the clinical findings; POEMS syndrome may cause organomegaly and sclerotic bone lesions but requires the presence of polyneuropathy or monoclonal paraproteinemia (often of lambda isotype). Secondary myelofibrosis is possible and would explain the organomegaly, cytopenias, and extramedullary hematopoiesis. However, the osteosclerosis pattern differs from ECD.1Prostate cancer characteristically causes asymmetric sclerotic bone metastasis and presents with pain. Myelophthisis presents with leucoerythroblastic changes (presence of nucleated red blood cells and myeloid precursors) in the peripheral blood smear and pancytopenia. Of note, none of the other 3 differential diagnoses would explain perinephric sclerosis in this case. ECD is an infrequent systemic histiocytic neoplasm, with a reported incidence of 0.35 per 1 000 000 adults.2Typically, ECD involves the perirenal spaces leading to the appearance of hairy kidneys in 50% to 60% of cases (Figure 1A). Sclerotic bone lesions are present in 95% of cases, classically seen in the metaphysis of the femurs bilaterally.3,4There is significant heterogeneity in clinical presentation with possible involvement of multiple sites, including the heart, retro-orbital space, large vessels (including aorta), central nervous system, and lungs. ECD is characterized by variants in the mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) pathway, most frequentlyBRAFV600E (approximately 50% of cases), while several others have been described.5,6Targeting the MAPK pathway is a major therapeutic advance in ECD, with high rates of response using BRAF/MEK inhibitors. Vemurafenib, a BRAF inhibitor, showed a response rate of 63% by Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tumors (RECIST) criteria and 100% by positron emission tomography/computed tomography, with a 2-year progression-free survival of 86%.7Similarly, cobimetinib (a MEK1/2 inhibitor) showed a response rate of 89% with durable responses inBRAFV600E–negative patients.8 The overlap of ECD or mixed histiocytosis and myeloid and myeloproliferative malignancies has been described in approximately 10% of cases.9Clonal hematopoiesis is frequent (15%) in patients with ECD, and specifically,TET2variants were associated with ECD harboringBRAFV600E, older age, and a retroperitoneal fibrosis phenotype, as seen in this case.10However, based on the available information, it is impossible to discern if the observedTET2andKRASvariants are part of the ECD or as a coexisting additional myeloid process. As highlighted by this case, the concomitant presence of perinephric fibrosis and symmetric sclerotic bone lesions should raise the concern for ECD. Given the clinical heterogeneity of this disease, ECD should be considered in any patient with perinephric fibrosis, symmetric sclerotic bone lesions, organomegaly, skin findings, or unexplained endocrine pituitary alterations. This patient elected for home hospice care after discussing the therapeutic options.

case_info.explanation: A perirenal biopsy showed infiltration of large atypical histocytes and dense fibrosis (Figure 2). These cells were positive for CD163, factor XIII, and CD14 and negative for CD1a and langerin. The perinephric tissue was positive for pathogenic variants inBRAFV600E,TET2, andKRAS. A bone marrow biopsy showed features of myeloproliferative neoplasm without significant fibrosis and an extensive infiltration by atypical histiocytes similar to those seen in the perinephric tissue. Based on these findings, a diagnosis of Erdheim-Chester disease (ECD) was established. The other options explain a fraction of the clinical findings; POEMS syndrome may cause organomegaly and sclerotic bone lesions but requires the presence of polyneuropathy or monoclonal paraproteinemia (often of lambda isotype). Secondary myelofibrosis is possible and would explain the organomegaly, cytopenias, and extramedullary hematopoiesis. However, the osteosclerosis pattern differs from ECD.1Prostate cancer characteristically causes asymmetric sclerotic bone metastasis and presents with pain. Myelophthisis presents with leucoerythroblastic changes (presence of nucleated red blood cells and myeloid precursors) in the peripheral blood smear and pancytopenia. Of note, none of the other 3 differential diagnoses would explain perinephric sclerosis in this case. ECD is an infrequent systemic histiocytic neoplasm, with a reported incidence of 0.35 per 1 000 000 adults.2Typically, ECD involves the perirenal spaces leading to the appearance of hairy kidneys in 50% to 60% of cases (Figure 1A). Sclerotic bone lesions are present in 95% of cases, classically seen in the metaphysis of the femurs bilaterally.3,4There is significant heterogeneity in clinical presentation with possible involvement of multiple sites, including the heart, retro-orbital space, large vessels (including aorta), central nervous system, and lungs. ECD is characterized by variants in the mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) pathway, most frequentlyBRAFV600E (approximately 50% of cases), while several others have been described.5,6Targeting the MAPK pathway is a major therapeutic advance in ECD, with high rates of response using BRAF/MEK inhibitors. Vemurafenib, a BRAF inhibitor, showed a response rate of 63% by Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tumors (RECIST) criteria and 100% by positron emission tomography/computed tomography, with a 2-year progression-free survival of 86%.7Similarly, cobimetinib (a MEK1/2 inhibitor) showed a response rate of 89% with durable responses inBRAFV600E–negative patients.8 The overlap of ECD or mixed histiocytosis and myeloid and myeloproliferative malignancies has been described in approximately 10% of cases.9Clonal hematopoiesis is frequent (15%) in patients with ECD, and specifically,TET2variants were associated with ECD harboringBRAFV600E, older age, and a retroperitoneal fibrosis phenotype, as seen in this case.10However, based on the available information, it is impossible to discern if the observedTET2andKRASvariants are part of the ECD or as a coexisting additional myeloid process. As highlighted by this case, the concomitant presence of perinephric fibrosis and symmetric sclerotic bone lesions should raise the concern for ECD. Given the clinical heterogeneity of this disease, ECD should be considered in any patient with perinephric fibrosis, symmetric sclerotic bone lesions, organomegaly, skin findings, or unexplained endocrine pituitary alterations. This patient elected for home hospice care after discussing the therapeutic options.
